title: La IA propone, el programa calcula y una persona firma
text:
Cuando una empresa quiere usar IA en un proceso, la conversación suele empezar por la herramienta. A mí me sirve más empezar por otra cosa: qué parte del proceso acepta un error y cuál no.
Un ejemplo de mi trabajo es una plataforma para contadores que ayuda a liquidar el impuesto de industria y comercio en Colombia. Cada municipio tiene sus tarifas, sus sanciones y su calendario, y todo eso cambia. El contador lee el acuerdo, depura la contabilidad del cliente, clasifica las actividades y llena un formulario renglón por renglón. Es lento, y una cifra mal puesta significa una multa. (Yo soy ingeniera, no contadora, y por eso la firma en este sistema nunca es mía ni del modelo.)
El trabajo está repartido en tres:

El modelo lee. Extrae tarifas, códigos y fechas de los acuerdos municipales y de los documentos del cliente, y los deja como propuesta.
Un programa calcula. Las cuentas las hace un motor con reglas escritas y probadas, con aritmética decimal exacta y el redondeo que pide la norma. Si lo corres dos veces con los mismos datos, da lo mismo.
Una persona aprueba. Nada llega a una declaración oficial sin que un contador lo revise y lo confirme.

Los modelos de lenguaje leen muy bien documentos desordenados, que era la parte lenta. Pero pueden leer un 5 donde hay un 6, y lo hacen con la misma seguridad con la que aciertan. Con este reparto, ese error aparece en una propuesta que alguien va a revisar antes de que exista un formulario.
También ayuda a saber quién responde. Si la cifra está mal, se puede ver si el documento se leyó mal, si la regla estaba mal escrita o si se aprobó sin revisar. Cuando un modelo hace los tres pasos, nadie puede contestar eso.
Si fuera a hacer lo mismo con otro proceso, marcaría cada paso con una letra: L si es leer o resumir, C si es calcular o aplicar una regla y D si es decidir. Los pasos L son buenos para empezar con IA, los C casi siempre necesitan un programa, y los D se quedan con una persona que tenga nombre. Se puede hacer con papel, y sirve para hablar de riesgos antes de comprar nada.

title: Un chatbot que puede decir «no tengo esa información»
text:
Trabajé en un chatbot para estudiantes de primer semestre. Preguntan por el reglamento, la matrícula, los calendarios y los servicios de bienestar, y las oficinas responden lo mismo cientos de veces. Un asistente puede ayudar mucho ahí, siempre que no invente. Si le dice a alguien un plazo que no existe, esa persona puede quedarse por fuera de un trámite.
Por eso casi todo el trabajo de diseño estuvo en lo que el bot no hace.
La primera decisión fue tener una sola base de conocimiento, verificada por la institución. El modelo responde con lo que encuentra ahí, y el prompt le prohíbe completar con lo que aprendió en su entrenamiento. Un modelo de lenguaje sabe muchas cosas sobre universidades en general, y en este caso eso es un problema, porque suena correcto y puede ser de otra universidad.
La segunda fue darle una salida. Cuando la base no tiene la respuesta, el bot dice «no tengo esa información». Cuando la pregunta se sale de su alcance, pasa el caso a una persona. Parece un detalle, pero un sistema sin esa opción queda obligado a responder algo.
La tercera fue probar con preguntas reales de estudiantes y corregir hasta que dejaron de aparecer respuestas inventadas en esas pruebas. Eso no garantiza que nunca vaya a pasar, y por eso la salida hacia una persona sigue ahí.
Usé la misma idea en otro sistema, uno que compara los documentos de un área de recursos humanos con un marco internacional. Si la búsqueda no encuentra un fragmento suficientemente relevante, el resultado es «no hay información suficiente», y al final se revisa que cada afirmación tenga un fragmento que la respalde. En un diagnóstico, un hallazgo inventado hace más daño que uno que falta.
Si estás montando un asistente en tu empresa o en tu universidad, yo empezaría por escribir la lista de preguntas que no debe responder y quién las recibe. Con esa lista lista, lo demás es más fácil.

title: More training, and the model did not improve
text:
In the summer of 2024 I did a research internship at TecNM Morelia, in Mexico, with Programa Delfín. I worked with Spanish clinical text, and one part of the project was to see if a language model could recover clinical words hidden in a note. It is a first step towards removing personal details from clinical text.
I compared a biomedical RoBERTa for Spanish with versions of the same model that I trained further on diabetes notes, using 100, 6,000 and 10,000 of them. The test had 101 notes, each with one clinical word masked by hand.

Exact recovery of the masked word, 101 notes. Wilson intervals, computed for this note.

The model without extra training had the highest score. In my portfolio I wrote that extra training lowered the score, and it is true for these notes. Looking at the intervals now, they overlap almost completely, and the difference between the first two rows is two notes out of 101. The same notes were used for every model, so a paired test on each answer would be more precise than these intervals, and I would need the individual answers to do it.
What I can say is that extra training showed no improvement on this test. I cannot say that it hurts.
There are three more limits I would fix before repeating it. The test notes were synthetic, written by GPT-3.5 in the style of a real case report, and real hospital notes have more abbreviations. Each note tested a single word. And exact match counts “enfermedad” as wrong when the hidden word was “diabetes”, although both fit the sentence.
If I repeated it, I would choose the size of the test before training and write down which difference is big enough to matter.
More about the project: Language models for Spanish clinical notes and the repository.

title: Fire Watch: the same event, written four ways
text:
At a tech event I learned about decision models for interfaces. Instead of writing text, they receive a situation and a closed list of options, and they return one option with a probability. Chrome is testing an API for this, the Decisions API, where the model runs on the computer of the person using the page.
I wanted to try the idea on something close to my work, so I made a small game. I lead the AI research of Kawsay, a wildfire detection project with FIRST Global Team Colombia, and the game borrows that setting. You read a message from a forest sensor and choose one of four actions: ignore, monitor, send a drone or call the brigade. The rule book is fixed, so there is always one correct answer.
Play Fire Watch

title: Fire Watch: the same event, written four ways
text:
The test
I made 24 events, six per action, and wrote each one in four ways: with numbers, in Spanish with numbers, in plain words, and in plain words again with one phrase changed. The event is the same in the four versions, so the answer should be the same too.

Numbers. Sensor at the east gate. Temperature 47 °C. Humidity 65%. Camera: no smoke.
Plain words. The battery was changed on Monday. At the east gate the air is very hot and humid as usual, and the camera shows nothing unusual.

title: Fire Watch: the same event, written four ways
text:
First results, in the cloud
I started with two general models in the cloud, asking them to pick one option from the list. I ran Claude Haiku 5.5 three times and Claude Sonnet 5.5 once.

Changing the language made no difference. Taking the numbers away did, for the smaller model. Almost every mistake went in the same direction: the rule book said monitor and the model said ignore. For an alarm this is the bad direction, because an event that needed attention gets no attention.

title: Fire Watch: the same event, written four ways
section: What I found in my own prompt
text:
What I found in my own prompt
The mistakes had something in common. My message said the camera shows “nothing unusual”, and my description of the ignore option ended with “Nothing is unusual”. The model may have been matching the words I repeated. In the fourth version I only changed that phrase to “no smoke”, and Haiku went from 19 or 20 to 22.
It is a small test with 24 events, one rule book and wording that I invented, and 22 is still not 24, so the repeated phrase does not explain everything. I would still check it in any product where a model chooses from a list, because the person who writes the options can push the answer without noticing.

title: Fire Watch: the same event, written four ways
text:
Next
The page can run the same decisions with a local model, through Chrome or with EmbeddingGemma 2 in the browser. That part is still experimental, and I will add the numbers here when I have them.
Code, and the answers of the last run of each model: lab/fire-watch. The game is a toy made to compare models. It is not a fire detection system.

title: When a model learns the scanner
text:
Medical imaging datasets are often put together from several hospitals, and each hospital has its own scanner. If most patients come from one scanner and most healthy people come from another, a model can get good results by recognizing the scanner, even if it learns little about the disease.
I wanted to see it with numbers, so I built the smallest experiment I could. It uses simulated images, needs only NumPy and runs in less than 15 seconds on my laptop.

title: When a model learns the scanner
text:
The images
Each image is a 32 × 32 gray ellipse, a very simple brain. People differ a little in size. Patients have a faint dark spot, and its position moves from one patient to another. The scanner adds a smooth change in brightness, so one side of the image is a bit brighter. I normalize the intensity of every image separately, which is a common step.



From left to right: control on scanner 0, patient on scanner 0, control on scanner 1, patient on scanner 1. It is hard to see either the spot or the shading by eye.

title: When a model learns the scanner
text:
The test
I trained a logistic regression on the pixels of 600 images, and I changed only one thing: how many of the patients came from scanner 1. At 50% the scanner says nothing about the disease. At 90%, nine out of ten patients come from scanner 1 and nine out of ten controls from scanner 0.
Then I tested the same model on 1,000 new people, in two ways. In the first one they had the same scanner mix as the training data, which is what a random split of the dataset gives you. In the second one the scanner had nothing to do with the disease. Every number is the mean of 10 runs.

title: When a model learns the scanner
text:
What I would check now
Before trusting an AUC on data from several sites, I would do three things.

Count patients and controls per scanner, and compute the AUC of the scanner label alone. If it is far from 0.5, a good result needs another explanation ruled out.
Report the AUC inside each scanner. It helps, but it did not show the whole problem here. At 90% it was 0.88, while the AUC with scanner unrelated to disease was 0.69, because the scanner also moves the scores up or down, so the scores of two people scanned on different machines can no longer be compared.
Test on people whose scanner is unrelated to the diagnosis, or on a site the model never saw.

title: When a model learns the scanner
section: The same thing with real images
text:
The same thing with real images
Zech and colleagues trained a network to find pneumonia in chest X-rays. Its AUC was 0.931 on new images from the hospitals used in training and 0.815 at another hospital. Sorting the images only by hospital already gave 0.861 (Zech et al. 2018). Glocker and colleagues worked with brain MRI from two studies, matched by age and sex, and a classifier could still tell the studies apart after careful preprocessing (Glocker et al. 2019).
My version is a toy. Real scanners differ in many more ways than one shading, real lesions are not round spots, and a logistic regression is not a deep network, so the exact numbers mean nothing outside this page. I used it to understand where the gap comes from, and changing the lesion and bias values in the code is a good way to play with it.
Code: experiment.py and figures.py.

title: Carolain Jiménez Bedoya
text:
I’m a systems engineer from Colombia working on medical image analysis and applied AI. I’m a research member of the MMV group at Universidad del Valle and lead AI engineering at S&S IP S.A.S. My first-author paper on traumatic brain injury and MRI was presented at CIARP 2025 (Springer LNCS). I care about methods that are measured honestly and reported next to their limits.
This is where I write about my research, the AI systems I build at work, and what I learn teaching and mentoring. Some notes are in English and some in Spanish.
